strengths: The paper investigates an important and challenging problem—non-invasive EMG-to-speech—and connects it to self-supervised speech representations, a timely direction for ACL.

The layer-wise linear probing analysis is the strongest part: it reports consistent correlations between SS audio features and EMG power (up to r=0.85) and identifies HuBERT layer 6 as a strong predictor, aligning with prior discrete-unit findings.

It compares multiple EMG feature representations (full covariance vec(E), diagonal power diag(E), and spectrogram bands B) on unit/phoneme decoding, finding covariance-based features more effective, which is a useful empirical observation.
It builds a sizable EMG speech corpus (~9 h, ~6,800 unique words, natural speaking rate) and an orofacial gesture dataset with synchronized audio, potentially valuable resources if released.
The gesture clustering analysis (70.6–73.7% k-medoids accuracy vs. 10% chance) provides evidence that EMG covariance/power features capture articulatory distinctions.
The paper is generally clear in its motivation and situates itself well relative to prior invasive and non-invasive speech neuroprosthesis work.
weaknesses: The headline claim—'synthesize speech'—is not supported by any synthesized-audio evaluation. The results stop at HuBERT-unit and phoneme error rates; no audio samples, no objective intelligibility (WER/CER), no perceptual quality (MOS/ABX), and no waveform examples are reported. The authors explicitly defer perceptual evaluation and WER/CER to 'continuing work,' so the main contribution remains unproven.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the EMG dataset and code are not available at review time ('will be made publicly available upon completion'), no repository or benchmark is provided, and many dataset/training details (number of speech participants, alignments, splits, hyperparameters) are missing. This prevents verification of the central analyses.

The synthesis architecture is unclear and arguably misdescribed: Tacotron is not a vocoder but an acoustic model, and how predicted discrete HuBERT units are converted to waveforms is not explained. The claim of 'without ... vocoder training' is misleading because a pretrained vocoder/acoustic model is still required.

The linear mapping evidence is correlational and may be confounded: since H and D(E) are obtained from temporally aligned speech and EMG for the same utterances, the high r=0.85 could reflect shared phonemic content rather than SS models encoding articulatory mechanisms per se. No controls for speaker, phoneme identity, shuffled alignment, or cross-subject generalization are reported.

The proposed role of EMG power as an intermediate representation is not actually tested: the synthesis model maps EMG features directly to HuBERT units, not EMG → EMG power → HuBERT units. Thus the link between the two main analyses is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Decoding performance is far from practical: PER ~41% and UER ~59% on the best feature representation, with no comparison to prior EMG-to-speech baselines or ablation of the TDS/CTC design. The lack of audio-level evaluation makes it impossible to judge whether the pipeline produces intelligible speech.

The gesture classification evaluation is limited: k-medoids accuracy is reported without statistical tests, confusion analysis, or cross-subject validation, and the T-SNE figure is for a single subject. The electrode configuration is also inconsistent (22 vs. 31 electrodes), complicating interpretation.

Several methodological details are underspecified, including how SS representations are pooled/aligned to EMG frames, how the linear regression is regularized, whether layers are compared with significance testing, and how many participants contributed to the main speech dataset. These omissions weaken the empirical claims.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: non-invasive EMG-to-speech conversion, with potential clinical impact for individuals who cannot use invasive brain-computer interfaces.
Introduces what appears to be a valuable large-vocabulary EMG speech corpus (approximately 9 hours, 6,800 unique words, 115 words per minute), which would be a useful resource if actually released.

Provides an interesting representational analysis showing that self-supervised speech features, especially HuBERT-base layer 6, can linearly predict EMG power vectors with r=0.85, and compares this across HuBERT, Wav2Vec2, and WavLM.
Reports gesture clustering results (k-medoids accuracy 70.6% using diagonal EMG power, 73.7% using full covariance) that support the separability of articulatory gestures in EMG feature space.
Compares multiple EMG input representations (vec(E), D(E), vec(B)) and shows that full covariance features yield the best unit and phoneme error rates, consistent with the paper's main hypothesis.
The sequence-to-sequence pipeline using TDS Conv, CTC, and a pretrained vocoder is clearly connected to prior alignment-free speech neuroprosthesis work, and the paper is generally readable.
weaknesses: The central claim of speech synthesis is not adequately supported: the paper reports only unit error rate (~58.7%) and phoneme error rate (~41.4%), with no intelligibility, perceptual quality, WER/CER, or audio samples. The authors explicitly defer perceptual evaluation and WER/CER to continuing work, so the stated aim of synthesizing speech remains unvalidated.

Reproducibility is insufficient: neither code nor data is available at review time, only a promise of future release. Critical experimental details are missing, including the number of speech participants, speaker-dependent vs. speaker-independent splits, optimizer settings, learning rates, model hyperparameters, CTC training details, and regularization for the linear probes.

The linear mapping evidence is weaker than claimed. The analysis tests H -> D(E) (a 31-dimensional diagonal summary) rather than a direct link to articulation or audio, and there are no control baselines such as shuffled features, random EMG, or subject-level analyses to rule out trivial temporal/acoustic correlations. The conclusion that SSL models 'implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms' is therefore overstated.

The speech synthesis evaluation lacks baselines and ablations: no comparison to prior EMG-to-speech systems, no random/majority baselines for UER/PER, no comparison across SSL layers or models for synthesis, and no evaluation of the actual audio output.

The empirical results are weak for a paper whose title promises speech synthesis: a 58.7% unit error rate and 41.4% phoneme error rate indicate the decoded sequences are far from usable, and there is no demonstration that the generated audio is intelligible.

Several methodological details are unclear or inconsistent, including the dimensionality of vec(E) and vec(B) (stated as 991 but not clearly derived from 31 electrodes), the distinction between the newly collected dataset and the adapted corpus from prior work, and the claim of 'without vocoder training' despite reliance on a pretrained vocoder.

The gesture clustering evidence is limited: only 13 orofacial movements from 12 participants in a separate dataset, no continuous-speech articulatory validation, and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals for the reported clustering and correlation results.

strengths: Introduces and open-sources significant EMG-to-speech resources, including a 9-hour healthy-speaker corpus with 6,800 unique words and a 1-hour ALS-speaker corpus, plus synthesized audio/transcripts, which is valuable for reproducible research.

Presents a clinically motivated alignment-free EMG-to-speech pipeline that leverages self-supervised speech models and a pretrained vocoder, avoiding explicit articulatory modeling and frame-level EMG-audio alignment.

Provides an interesting probing analysis showing that EMG power representations can be linearly predicted from S3 speech representations (r = 0.85) and that articulatory gestures form separable clusters, alongside layer-wise analyses across HuBERT, Wav2Vec2, and WavLM.

Demonstrates that phoneme-guided decoding and consistency training improve HuBERT unit decoding over a unit-only CTC baseline (e.g., 51.81 vs 56.08 UER on DATA_GENERAL and 46.98 vs 52.29 on DATA_ALS).
Includes human evaluation with WER, PER, and MOS, gives substantial implementation detail in appendices, and discusses limitations and ethical considerations transparently.
weaknesses: The central claim that S3 representations are strongly linearly related to EMG power rests on a single healthy participant and same-session data; no cross-subject or cross-session validation is provided, so generalizability remains unclear.

The linear probing uses a low-dimensional diagonal covariance proxy D(E) rather than full vec(E), and lacks controls such as time-shuffled or misaligned audio; the reported r = 0.85 may partly reflect temporal alignment and shared phonetic structure rather than a deep articulatory mapping.

Speech synthesis results are modest (about 62.55% WER on the large-vocabulary healthy set and 50.82% WER on the ALS set), and the paper cannot make direct same-dataset comparisons to prior EMG-to-speech systems because of differing alignment assumptions, corpora, and vocoding setups.

The synthesis target units are derived from Google TTS audio from transcripts rather than from the participants' actual speech; WER therefore measures match to generic TTS-derived linguistic content, and MOS may reflect vocoder naturalness more than EMG decoding quality.

The ALS evaluation includes only one participant with 60 test sentences, with no speaker-independent split or confidence intervals; the clinical claim of broader usability for ALS or dysarthria is therefore not yet substantiated.

Some methodological controls are missing, including a shuffled-audio baseline for linear probing, stronger feature-representation baselines for synthesis, and a more rigorous comparison to isolate the contribution of S3 targets versus the encoder architecture.

The framing around a 'first quantitative relationship' and comparisons with prior work would benefit from more cautious calibration, since the evidence supports a promising but preliminary finding rather than a firmly established general property.
